newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish bonos dive amid fears of possible EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: Spanish bonos dive amid fears of possible EMU delay.

text.p: Spanish debt tumbled on Friday, with long-term futures losing more than two points on fears of a possible delay in European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Dealers said declines could continue next week despite expected remarks from Italian and Spanish politicians this weekend lending the market support.
Earlier on Friday, Germany's Bundesbank denied any possibility of delaying EMU, but the market remained worried and sold government debt.
Peripheral bonds were further gripped by fears Italy may have problems meeting convergence criteria if Italy's mini-budget has difficulty passing.

"There are two issues. First, more doubts over Germany and then, difficulties for Italy. And we are still thinking that if Italy doesn't enter, Spain won't make it either," said Henrik Lumholdt, economist of Bank of America in Madrid.

The long-term futures contract ended at 111.70, losing 209 basis points. The 10-year bond cash spread moved back to 145 basis points, its level in mid-November, from a record low 83 basis points made at the end of January.
"All this was prompted by the prospect of an EMU delay," said Mark Geddes at 4cast in London.
"Over the weekend, it's likely we'll see the Italian and the Spanish press full of EMU-friendly comments. But what we need are positive German politicians' remarks," Geddes said.

Next week, German February unemployment data will be key. If jobless rises from January's record, German difficulties in meeting EMU criteria would be highlighted and make an EMU delay seem more likely.
Domestically, Spain's Treasury auctions of 3-, 5-, 10- and 15-years bonds on Tuesday and Wednesday could further depress the market, dealers added.

The Spanish Treasury recently said its big current account with the Bank of Spain of 2.53 trillion pesetas ($17.6 billion) at the end of December, up sharply from 1.56 trillion 12 months ago, suggested it could reduce the size of the offer if market conditions deteriorated.
But "when the market is domestically-driven, like now, and domestic investors start to sell their own market, that means the market is really falling," said Geddes.
Though a few dealers said the market could correct higher on Monday, none were willing to make any precise forecasts after so many technical support levels failed on Friday.
In the afternoon, the long-term futures contract broke several supports, including 112.80, 112.60 and 112.20 before triggering stop-losses and hitting a 111.61 low, dealers said.
"Today, we had a 'mini-crisis,' with the lira around 1,000 versus the mark and the peseta trading at around 85 per mark," said a dealer in Madrid.
The Bank of Spain was reported to have bought pesetas several times on to defend the currency.
After hours, the peseta was trading in New York at 84.94/96 per mark at 1730 GMT.
